prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength made timekeeping at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from the Higgs discovery (B003) to optical lattice clocks (B025), with Katori and Ye. My round-1 position was explicitly conditional: I would hold B003 only if the expert reports could support the three spokespersons as the right names. Nothing in the exchange supports them. Lindroth and Mehlig independently find the proxy unconvincing, nobody else ranks B003 first, and I cannot honestly claim that Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee are the people who made the decisive contribution among thousands. The discovery is as large as I said, but a prize needs a defensible who as well as a what, and here it does not exist. B025 is the best case on the shortlist on that second criterion. The idea is distinct: trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the light shift cancels. Its accuracy near 10^-18 is reproduced and cross-compared between national laboratories, and the two names are matched by every member who prefers it. I was most sceptical of it on the question whether the clock has told us something about nature or only about our instruments. The colleagues have shifted me partly. Comparing clock heights across a millimetre-scale cloud is a test of the gravitational redshift in a regime nobody could reach before, and the bounds on drifting constants and on ultralight dark matter are results about the world, even though they are so far null. As someone who has argued that string theory needs clues from nature, I find null results from a controlled laboratory device more instructive than elegant claims with no test at all. I would require that the citation be drawn around the lattice clock only.
statement.case_against: My original objection stands in a weaker form: the physics output so far is bounds and capability, not a surprise, and a committee that wants a discovery in the narrowest sense will find B036 stronger. The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize is real, because Ye's clocks depend on the comb, and the citation must say what is new. The credit also has gaps: Takamoto, Lemonde and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups have claims that nobody on the committee has checked against the priority record, and I am relying on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson for details of the atomic physics. If the experts show that the first demonstration of the strontium lattice clock does not belong to Katori's group, the two names would need to change. Finally, a two-person metrology prize in a year with strong condensed-matter candidates may seem a modest use of the prize to some colleagues, and I do not dismiss that.

responses.point: He argues that the lattice clock is a new capability with downstream physics (constants, geodesy, millimetre-scale redshift, dark matter) and that Takamoto's strontium demonstration is part of Katori's own credit.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me most. In round 1 I called the clock capability and not discovery. Your point that the redshift across a millimetre-scale sample and the limits on varying constants are physics outputs is fair, and I accept it as sufficient for a prize, provided the citation says so. On Takamoto I think your reading is plausible, but it is not established. A single group's claim is exactly what the experts should check, and I agree with Olsson that the original demonstration is the test and not the most precise one. Your disclosure about John Hall is, in my view, a matter of disclosure and not recusal, since a mentor lineage without collaboration is how most of us are connected to the field. I leave the final judgement to the Chair.

responses.point: She ranks B025 first, wants the citation tied to the magic-wavelength lattice and its record-accuracy demonstration, and says the priority of the Sr work is not fully settled. She also ranked the Higgs discovery eighth because of collaboration credit.
responses.response: On B003 you were right and I have moved, for the reason you gave: awkward attribution is not a minor matter if the names are only proxies. I still hold that this is a point about credit and not about the importance of the discovery. For B025 I agree that the citation should name the lattice clock and its accuracy, and not clocks in general, so that we do not need to settle the priority of Takamoto and Lemonde, and I would keep Th-229 out. I would like your view on whether the blackbody and lattice light-shift evaluation really supports the stated 10^-18 uncertainty, as the Chair asks, because I cannot assess that part myself.

responses.point: He agrees that nature should lead and that B003 has an attribution problem, but moved to B036 because the HgTe edge conductance followed a sharp prediction, and he questions what is new in B025 beyond a long sequence of accuracy improvements.
responses.response: I agree that B036 fits the nature-first criterion and I listed it as my fallback for that reason. On the clock I share your doubt about improvement versus discovery, but I think the answer is the magic-wavelength condition itself, which was a conceptual step, and the many-body regime that came after it. I do not agree that Shoucheng Zhang's death makes the trio less arbitrary: Hughes and Bernevig are alive, and a trio that omits the authors of the prediction that Molenkamp tested leaves an obvious question. That is why I do not put B036 first, even though the physics is the stronger on my own criterion of surprise.

responses.point: He prefers B036 for the theory-plus-experiment chain with stable interpretation, accepts that Bernevig and Hughes are omitted, and would rather not stretch the prize to add names.
responses.response: I put B036 as my first alternative and I agree with you that the Z2 class is distinct from the 2016 prize, since it needs no magnetic field. The difficulty is the one you acknowledge. With a three-name limit, Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leave out the BHZ prediction, and the committee would carry a visible gap into every discussion afterwards. A clean two-name credit is less dramatic than a theory-meets-experiment story, but it is the one I can defend without caveats. If the group concludes that the omission of Bernevig and Hughes is tolerable, I could accept B036 as the single part, and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: He moved from IceCube to B025, asks whether the committee can defend its credit, and says the lattice-clock citation should name the clock itself.
responses.response: We both moved from a field we know to one we rely on colleagues for, and I think we should say so openly in the record. I agree with your request that the lattice clock itself be named. On IceCube, I accept your answer that the Baikal and AMANDA question concerns the names and not whether the discovery stands, but timing still matters. A prize before source populations are established invites the same uncertainty about the credited names that sank B003 for me.

uncertainties: Whether the experts can confirm that Katori's group first demonstrated the Sr lattice clock, or whether Takamoto, Lemonde or another group should alter the two names.
Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct achievement from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion prize, which depends on how the citation is drawn.
Whether the 10^-18 uncertainty budget (blackbody, lattice light shift) is as robust as the supporters say; I rely on Lindroth and Kroll for this.
Whether the committee would rather reward the more surprising physics of B036 despite the omission of Bernevig and Hughes.
statement.conflict_note: I am the Secretary and a string theorist with no personal or institutional link to Katori, Ye or any other shortlisted candidate. David Gross, my PhD supervisor, is not on the shortlist. Kroll's connection to John Hall's laboratory is, in my view, a disclosure matter and not a ground for recusal; the Chair decides. I rely on the atomic-physics members for the technical details of B025 and have no independent expertise there.
